items.prompt: What is "calibration"?
choices: A meeting where multiple managers compare their reports' cases against each other and against a shared bar, rather than one manager deciding unilaterally
A one-on-one meeting between a manager and their report to discuss goals
A rubber stamp on whatever an individual manager has already decided
A written self-assessment an employee fills out about their own performance
items.explanation: Calibration is specifically a cross-manager comparison process — not a 1:1, not a self-assessment, and not a rubber stamp on one manager's existing decision.
items.reference:
Calibration
👥 Multiple managers compare cases
📏 ...against each other and a shared bar
Why: it's a cross-manager check, not one manager's unilateral call.
items.learnMore:
Why calibration exists at all

Calibration exists because a single manager, however well-intentioned, is a biased judge of their own report — they know the person, like them (usually), and have no comparison point against other cases in the same cycle. Putting multiple managers' cases side by side, against the same documented bar, is what catches both unconscious favoritism and plain inconsistency between levels.

Common mistake

Assuming calibration is a rubber-stamp formality. Its entire function is to be a real check, not a ceremony.

items.explanation: L1 uses exactly this framing — support is necessary to start a case, but not sufficient on its own to guarantee the outcome.
items.reference:
Necessary, not sufficient
🟢 Manager's support: starts the case
🔒 Still has to survive the room
Why: support gets a case into the process; it can't finish the process alone.
items.learnMore:
A common logical pattern

"Necessary but not sufficient" shows up anywhere a single factor is required to even attempt something, but other independent factors can still block the outcome. A manager's support is necessary — without it, no packet is even written — but it isn't sufficient, because the packet still has to clear a rubric and compete for slots that the manager doesn't fully control.

items.prompt: What is a "promotion packet"?
choices: The written case a manager submits into calibration on a report's behalf
A folder of an employee's past performance reviews
A verbal pitch a manager gives from memory during calibration
A survey filled out by an employee's peers
items.explanation: A promotion packet is specifically the written case submitted into calibration — not a review folder, a verbal pitch, or a peer survey.
items.reference:
Promotion packet
📄 The written case submitted into calibration
🔍 What's actually evaluated in the room
Why: verbal enthusiasm doesn't travel into calibration — only the packet does.
items.learnMore:
Why it has to be written

A promotion packet exists specifically so a case can be evaluated by people who weren't there for the work — writing it down is what makes it portable and checkable. A verbal case, however sincere, only exists in the room where it's spoken; a written packet can be read, questioned, and compared against a rubric by managers who have no other way to access the evidence.

items.prompt: What is a "leveling bar" (rubric)?
choices: The documented, level-specific expectations a packet's evidence is measured against
The number of years someone has worked at a company
An informal sense each manager has of who deserves a promotion
A fixed salary number attached to each job title
items.explanation: The leveling bar is specifically the documented expectations evidence is measured against — not tenure, an informal sense, or a salary figure.
items.reference:
Leveling bar (rubric)
📐 Documented, level-specific expectations
✅/❌ What a packet's evidence is measured against
Why: without a documented bar, 'strong enough' is just an opinion.
items.learnMore:
Slot/budget constraints are a separate thing

The rubric answers "did this case clear the bar"; a slot or budget constraint answers an entirely different question — "is there room to approve it this cycle, regardless of quality." Keeping these two concepts distinct is what lets an engineer ask the right follow-up question when a promotion doesn't happen: which one failed, the case or the capacity?

🗣️ "I'm pushing hard for your promo"
😕 "It didn't happen this time" — no further detail

items.learnMore:
Why vague feedback is genuinely ambiguous

"It didn't happen this time" is consistent with two completely different situations: the packet didn't clear the rubric, or the packet cleared the rubric but lost to a slot constraint. From the engineer's side, both produce the identical sentence back from their manager — which is exactly why L3 teaches a specific follow-up question designed to tell the two apart, rather than treating the vague phrase as self-explanatory.

items.prompt: Per L2, why do claims like "doing well" or "ready for the next level" tend to collapse under direct questioning in calibration?

items.explanation: L2 explains that vague impressions collapse specifically because there's no checkable evidence to fall back on when questioned.
items.reference:
Impressions vs. checkable claims
💭 "Doing well" — collapses under a direct question

Why: a stranger to the work needs something they can independently evaluate.
items.learnMore:
What makes a claim survive scrutiny

"Doing well" fails the moment a skeptical manager asks "compared to what, specifically?" — there's no fact behind it to answer with. A claim survives the same question when it names something concrete: a project, a number, a before/after. This is the same distinction L3's rewritten packet makes explicit with the 2.1%-to-0.3% error-rate example.

items.prompt: Per L3, why does the rewritten packet's specific error-rate number (2.1% to 0.3%) matter more than saying "greatly improved reliability"?
choices: A specific number is falsifiable — a skeptical manager could in principle check it — while a vague claim asks to be taken on faith
Specific numbers are required by law in every promotion packet
Percentages are always more impressive than any other kind of evidence, regardless of context

items.explanation: L3 explains the number matters because it's falsifiable and checkable, unlike a vague claim that requires trusting the writer's judgment.
items.reference:
Falsifiable vs. vague
🔢 "2.1% to 0.3%" — checkable, falsifiable
💭 "Greatly improved" — asks to be taken on faith
Why: a specific number can in principle be checked; a vague claim can't.
items.learnMore:
Falsifiability is the actual mechanism

A number like "2.1% to 0.3%" is falsifiable — a skeptical manager could in principle go verify it, which is exactly why it survives questioning better than an adjective. This isn't about numbers being more impressive; a precise, checkable claim that turns out modest still beats an impressive-sounding claim nobody can verify, because calibration specifically rewards evidence that doesn't require trusting the writer.

items.prompt: A packet says: "She is doing great and everyone trusts her." What is missing?

items.reference: Committee = the group reviewing cases. Checkable evidence = examples, numbers, artifacts, or outcomes someone else can inspect.
items.learnMore:
What a committee can do with a plain sentence

"Doing great and everyone trusts her" gives a committee a conclusion with no path to check it — there's no project, no number, no outcome to ask a follow-up about. The fix isn't to make the sentence longer or more emphatic; it's to replace the conclusion with the specific fact that would lead a reader to that conclusion on their own, the same move L3's rewritten packet makes with its error-rate and mentoring examples.

items.prompt: If the packet cleared the bar but lost because of promotion slots, what is the most useful next step?
choices: Ask whether the packet can be preserved or resubmitted next cycle, while checking if any evidence should be updated
Assume the case was weak and start over from zero
Stop documenting evidence because the process is random
Ask only whether the manager personally supported the case
items.explanation: A slot-constrained strong case needs a different response than a weak case. Preserve the evidence, ask what should be refreshed, and confirm the path for the next cycle.
items.reference: If the case was not ready, build better evidence. If it was ready but there was no room, the next move is timing, preservation, and resubmission.
items.learnMore:
Two different next steps for two different problems

Treating a slot-constrained case the same way as a weak case wastes the work already done — the evidence that cleared the bar doesn't need to be rebuilt from scratch, it needs to be preserved and carried into the next cycle. The direct question from L3 (bar vs. slots) is what tells you which of these two very different next steps actually applies.
